articles.title: After South Africa tour snub, Shreyanka Patil earns India A call for England series - India Today
articles.summary: After South Africa tour snub, Shreyanka Patil earns India A call for England series India Today
articles.content: Shreyanka Patil has earned a place in the India A squads for the upcoming home series against England A, giving the off-spinner an opportunity to get back into contention after missing out on recent international assignments.The 23-year-old has been named in all three squads for the T20, one-day and multi-day matches. Her selection comes after she missed India's series against Zimbabwe and was also overlooked for the upcoming multi-format tour of South Africa.Patil has made a strong case for her return with impressive performances in domestic cricket. Representing Karnataka in the Senior Women's T20 Trophy, she has registered two five-wicket hauls in successive matches.She picked up 526 against Maharashtra on October 27 to help Karnataka secure a seven-wicket victory. Two days later, she produced another impressive spell, claiming 518 against Goa as Karnataka registered a four-wicket win.MUMBAI INDIANS STARS PICKED FOR INDIA AThe England A series will also provide an opportunity for several young players to showcase their talent. Sanika Chalke and Akshita Bhagat, who recently secured contracts at the 2027 Women's Premier League (WPL) auction, have both been named in the India A squads.Both players were picked up by Mumbai Indians for Rs 10 lakh each. Chalke, a batter, features in the T20 squad, while all-rounder Bhagat has been included in the one-day and multi-day squads.Anushka Sharma will lead India A in the T20 and one-day matches, with Minnu Mani serving as her deputy in both formats. Mani will captain the side in the multi-day fixture, with Tejal Hasabnis named vice-captain.The tour will begin with a three-match T20 series in Pune from November 30 to December 5. articles.title: India's Niraj Kumar Wins Bronze in Men's 50m 3-Position, Secures 2028 LA Olympics Quota - Deccan Chronicle
articles.summary: India's Niraj Kumar Wins Bronze in Men's 50m 3-Position, Secures 2028 LA Olympics Quota Deccan Chronicle
articles.content: Doha: India's Niraj Kumar secured a quota place for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics after clinching bronze in the men's 50m rifle 3-positions event at the ISSF World Championships here on Wednesday.It was India's second Olympic quota at the championships, following Jaypal Malviya's silver in the men's 10m air pistol event a few days ago.Niraj finished with 346.5 points. He was in contention for silver but a 9.4 in the closing stages pushed him down to third place.Individual Neutral Athlete (AIN) Dmitrii Pimenov claimed the gold with a world junior record score of 362.8, while Slovakia's Patrik Jany took silver. Both also secured their Olympic quota places.The other Indian in the final, Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar, finished fifth with 323.7 points.

articles.title: Aaryavir Sehwag's old interview with Virat Kohli goes viral after U19 Asia Cup heroics - India Today
articles.summary: Aaryavir Sehwag's old interview with Virat Kohli goes viral after U19 Asia Cup heroics India Today
articles.content: Almost nine years after he sat across Virat Kohli with a microphone in his hand, Aaryavir Sehwag is making headlines of his own. A video of the youngster interviewing Kohli in 2017 has resurfaced after the son of former India opener Virender Sehwag struck a memorable 160 in the Under-19 Asia Cup.Aaryavir, who was a young child when he interviewed the then India captain across all three formats for Star Sports, has since taken his first significant steps in age-group cricket. His innings against the UAE on Monday helped India register a 70-run victory and secure a place in the semi-finals.The 19-year-old scored 160 off 168 deliveries, striking 17 fours and seven sixes. He shared a 193-run partnership with VK Vineeth, who contributed 67, as India posted 309 for seven.As his innings attracted attention, the old interview with Kohli began circulating on social media, offering a glimpse of Aaryavir's early admiration for one of India's most influential batters.During the interaction, Aaryavir asked Kohli about his first meeting with Virender Sehwag. Kohli recalled meeting the former India opener in Delhi through a state-level coach who knew both cricketers. The meeting had taken place after Kohli had scored his first double century in Under-17 cricket.Aaryavir also asked Kohli about the now-famous photograph of Ashish Nehra presenting a trophy to the former India captain as a teenager.Kohli also spoke about his journey in the game and encouraged the youngster to dream big and believe in his abilities.Aaryavir has previously spoken about his admiration for Kohli's approach to batting. In an interaction ahead of the tournament, he spoke about wanting to incorporate aspects of the former India captain's game into his own.The knock against the UAE was Aaryavir's maiden Youth ODI century. He had also impressed earlier in the competition, scoring an unbeaten 72 against Nepal.While his famous surname inevitably brings expectations, Aaryavir is beginning to carve out his own identity in age-group cricket.The youngster will be in focus when India take on Afghanistan in the U19 Asia Cup semifinal on Thursday in Oman.- Ends

articles.title: Groundsman Lee Fortis, who clashed with Gambhir, leaves Surrey after disciplinary row - India Today
articles.summary: Groundsman Lee Fortis, who clashed with Gambhir, leaves Surrey after disciplinary row India Today
articles.content: Lee Fortis, Surrey's head groundsman who was involved in a heated confrontation with India head coach Gautam Gambhir during the team's 2025 Test tour of England, has left the county club following disciplinary proceedings over his conduct.Fortis, who had been Surrey's head groundsman for more than a decade, was placed on indefinite leave in July after an altercation with an England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) employee at The Oval. The incident took place a day before MI London faced London Spirit in The Hundred at the venue. He also had a heated exchange with Surrey chief executive Steve Elworthy following the incident and did not return to work for the remainder of the summer.Fortis' LinkedIn profile now indicates that he left Surrey in October and is open to work. A Surrey spokesperson confirmed his departure to Telegraph Sport, saying: "Lee Fortis has left the club and we wish him well for the future."The findings of the disciplinary proceedings have not been made public. The Cricket Regulator was also reported to have opened an investigation into the July incident but did not comment when approached by Telegraph Sport. There has been no official confirmation that Fortis was dismissed by Surrey.Fortis had previously attracted considerable attention in July 2025 when he clashed with Gambhir ahead of the fifth and final Test between India and England at The Oval. The disagreement arose during an Indian training session, with the groundsman unhappy about the team's use of the main square and the handling of equipment near the pitch.The exchange was caught on camera, with Gambhir visibly confronting Fortis. "You can go and report to whoever you want, but you can't tell us what to do. You don't tell us what to do, you're just a groundsman," the India head coach was heard saying.India batting coach Sitanshu Kotak subsequently criticised the manner in which the groundstaff had communicated with the visiting team, describing Fortis as arrogant. He said the coaching staff had been asked to maintain a distance of 2.5 metres from the wicket while inspecting the surface.Fortis, however, played down the confrontation when approached by Indian media, saying there was nothing to speak about and nothing to hide.The 40-year-old joined Surrey in 2012 and became one of the most recognisable figures in English county cricket. His work at The Oval earned him the ECB Grounds Manager of the Year award for three successive years, from 2022 to 2024. Surrey also won the County Championship in each of those seasons.His departure comes at a significant time for the club, with The Oval scheduled to host the World Test Championship final in June 2027 and the fifth Ashes Test later that summer. Surrey will now have to find a replacement for a groundsman who had overseen its playing surfaces for more than a decade.- Ends

articles.title: Meet Ishan Sood: India's U19 pacer taught by his dad, YouTube and ChatGPT - India Today
articles.summary: Meet Ishan Sood: India's U19 pacer taught by his dad, YouTube and ChatGPT India Today
articles.content: For six to nine months, Ishan Sood bowled one delivery. A good length, aimed at the top of off-stump, the same ball again and again, with a single cricket ball for company. He and his father, Dheeraj, practised nothing else.That patience is now on show at the Under-19 Asia Cup, where the 17-year-old from Morinda, Punjab, has become one of the more interesting young quicks to watch. At 6 feet 4 inches, Ishan has the sort of frame that makes a fast bowler stand out before he has delivered a ball. Eight wickets in three matches tell part of the story. The manner in which he has taken them tells the rest.Against Nepal, he bowled 10 overs, four of them maidens, and conceded just 18 runs for three wickets. Against Pakistan came a disciplined 1 for 36 in nine overs. Against the UAE he produced the best figures of the three: four wickets for 37 runs in seven overs.What catches the eye is the control, more than the height or the bounce. He keeps returning to the corridor of uncertainty, targeting the top of off-stump and making batters play. He can swing the ball both ways. Bowling from a wide angle to a right-hander, he can also straighten it after pitching, which beats most batters at will. There is a useful yorker too. For a young fast bowler, there is already a fair bit to work with.Social media has begun comparing him with Ishant Sharma: the height, the lanky frame, the ball that straightens after pitching. It is an early comparison, and Ishan has a long way to go. But how he got here is the more unusual story. Is Ishan the new Ishant? (Photo: Instagram)There is no elaborate coaching set-up and no permanent specialist overseeing every aspect of his bowling. For years it has largely been a two-man operation, Ishan and his father. Their classroom has been the cricket ground, but also YouTube, Google, social media and, more recently, ChatGPT.They watch, research, swap videos and talk it through. A particular delivery catches their attention, and they work out how it is bowled, when it can be used and whether it might suit Ishan. Sometimes it is a bowling variation. At other times it could be a gym exercise, a nutritional requirement or a technical adjustment.“We rely a lot on social media, YouTube, Google and ChatGPT. We research things and discuss them with each other. We share videos, point out what a particular bowler is doing and work out what we need to learn or practise,” Dheeraj tells IndiaToday.in.This is not a case of watching a fast bowler on a screen and copying his action. Father and son spend time understanding why a delivery works, where it should be bowled and how it can fit into Ishan’s game. The back-of-the-hand slower ball was one they learnt exactly that way.“We research almost everything, from nutrition and gym training to bowling techniques. Whatever we need to learn, we look it up on social media and study it in detail. We try to understand every aspect of his development,” Dheeraj says. Ishan Sood with his father Dheeraj. (Photo: Special arrangement)For a father who played club-level cricket himself, it has become close to a full-time pursuit. Dheeraj bowled fast and grew up admiring Allan Donald and Glenn McGrath. He never progressed to the state level, something he partly puts down to the lack of sporting support available in his playing days. He wanted his sons to have a different experience.His elder son also wanted to become a cricketer, but an injury cut short that ambition. He had been sent elsewhere for training, and the setback changed the family’s plans. With Ishan, Dheeraj decided he would take charge himself. There would be no permanent coach. He would accompany his younger son to practice and oversee his development.It came at a cost. When Ishan was around 13, Dheeraj sold his garment showroom to devote more time and resources to his son’s cricket.“I didn’t know beforehand that he would become a good fast bowler. I knew I would make him one!” Dheeraj says, laughing.His own cricketing ambitions had not gone as far as he would have liked. His elder son’s journey had ended prematurely. Ishan would get every opportunity the family could provide.NINE MONTHS, ONE DELIVERYThe training was built on repetition rather than variety. For months, father and son worked on a single delivery: a good length, aimed at the top of off-stump. The idea was to make Ishan so comfortable bowling that ball, over and over, that he would never lose his line or length.“We spent a long time working on just one thing: bowling a good length, targeting the top of off-stump. We spent six to nine months concentrating on that delivery, using just one ball,” Dheeraj says.Only after Ishan had mastered that length did they move on to developing movement in both directions.“He already had natural swing and seam movement. Once he mastered that length, we worked on bringing the ball in and taking it away from the same spot. We spent another eight or nine months on that. We did not practise anything else during that period.”Yorkers came later, and took far less time. Dheeraj was struck by how quickly his son picked up the delivery.“After that, we moved on to yorkers. We practised them for 10 to 15 days, and within 16 days, he had become very good at bowling them. He is a very quick learner.”The emphasis on one length, and on movement from the same spot, is now visible in Ishan’s bowling. His height helps him extract bounce, but he is not simply looking to hurry batters with pace. He wants them to commit to a shot, and then he makes the ball do something different. Ishan Sood idolises Glenn McGrath. (Photo: Instagram)IMPRESSIVE NUMBERS AT 17The age-group record suggests the method has worked. In the 2024-25 Vijay Merchant Trophy, playing Under-16 cricket, Ishan picked up 28 wickets in seven matches. He averaged 17.64, conceded just 2.36 runs per over and bowled 68 maidens across 1,003 deliveries.He carried that form into the Under-19 Vinoo Mankad Trophy. Last year he took 20 wickets in eight matches and finished as the tournament’s leading wicket-taker, with Punjab reaching the final. This year, Punjab went one step further. Ishan played a key role in bowling them to victory, with a four-wicket haul against Mumbai in the final in Indore in October.His performances brought opportunities with the India Under-19 side, including the Challenger Trophy and the triangular series. Missing the previous Asia Cup and World Cup cycle was a setback. He returned to the India set-up through the tour of Sri Lanka in June-July, where he played two matches, and attended the Under-19 High Performance Camp at the Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru.He has also had the chance to work with former India fast bowler VRV Singh, India’s Under-19 bowling coach. Ishan says Singh’s backing and the time spent working with him have been valuable.“Our bowling coach VRV Singh has been backing me a lot. We had two sessions, which helped me a lot,” Ishan said during the tournament.The confidence from Punjab’s Vinoo Mankad Trophy triumph has carried into the Asia Cup as well. Asked about the impact of winning an Under-19 tournament, Ishan acknowledged its importance.“Yes, winning an U19 tournament helps you with confidence,” he said.Another family member has helped keep the journey on course. Ishan’s elder brother, now 21, has taken over much of the responsibility of managing the family’s travel agency. He also helps with household affairs and often accompanies Ishan to gym sessions, physiotherapy and bowling practice. Ishan Sood has impressed in age-group cricket. (Photo: Instagram)MATURE, FAST LEARNERIshan has been noticed well beyond the family, by the Centre of Excellence and the selectors. In Punjab, Sandeep Sawal, coach of Amritsar Soormas in the inaugural Sher-e-Punjab T20 league, had watched Ishan in state-level tournaments over the years and liked what he saw: a tall fast bowler who already understood his craft.When the league auction came up, Ishan was injured. Sawal backed the youngster anyway. The opportunity that followed let Ishan spend time at Soormas with the likes of Abhishek Sharma and Naman Dhir.Sawal has followed Ishan’s development since, and believes there is more to him than the physical attributes. What impresses him most is the youngster’s ability to read conditions and make adjustments.“He understands line and length and knows what to bowl in different situations. He reads the pitch well. Even on slower surfaces, he knows when to use cutters. He understands field placements and has a good sense of the game,” Sawal tells IndiaToday.in.Sawal likes what he has seen of Ishan's bowling, but believes the youngster still has work to do on the physical front.“He has to keep playing, build muscle and improve his fitness. There is also scope to work on his bowling action and increase his pace,” he says. Ishan needs to work on getting physically stronger, feels one of his coaches. (Photo: Instagram)Even now, Dheeraj remains closely involved in Ishan’s training. They continue to watch videos, discuss bowling techniques and look for ways to improve. The routine that began in Morinda has not changed much, even as Ishan has moved on to the India Under-19 team.Dheeraj’s ambitions for his son are not restricted to limited-overs cricket either. If anything, he says, Ishan is drawn to the longest format.“The real joy of cricket lies in watching Test matches. True cricket lovers enjoy Test cricket, and Ishan loves playing it,” he says.The boy Dheeraj took to the nets in Morinda is now troubling batters at the Under-19 Asia Cup.- Ends

articles.title: India's Pollution Crisis Hits Sports: Chennai Open Tennis Final Postponed Amid Heavy Smog - Business Today
articles.summary: India's Pollution Crisis Hits Sports: Chennai Open Tennis Final Postponed Amid Heavy Smog Business Today
articles.content: India's post-Diwali pollution surge has disrupted more than just daily life. The Chennai Open women's singles final between defending champion Janice Tien and Magda Linette was postponed after rain delays were followed by heavy smoke from Diwali fireworks engulfing the stadium. Tien shared an Instagram story showing the smog and an AQI reading of 1,556, raising fresh concerns over the conditions at the venue. The incident adds to a growing list of sporting events affected by India's pollution crisis, including cricket fixtures that have faced postponements or venue changes amid poor air quality. As the Chennai Open approaches its final edition, the disruption has cast a shadow over the tournament's farewell.

articles.title: What is the Gokul Cooperative Milk Federation election issue in Maharashtra? | Explained - The Hindu
articles.summary: What is the Gokul Cooperative Milk Federation election issue in Maharashtra? | Explained The Hindu
articles.content: Election to one of Maharashtra’s largest milk federations has turned into a political slugfest. Kolhapur Zilla Sahakari Dudh Utpadak Sangh Ltd, known as Gokul, is one of Maharashtra’s largest and most influential dairy co-operatives. After the election to the directors’ positions was held recently, the Congress-led panel won by a wafer-thin majority of 13-12 in a body of 25 directors. Soon thereafter, the BJP-led State government passed an order to appoint five nominated directors. Four of them will have voting rights. This caused a massive backlash, as it will tilt the majority in favour of the ruling alliance via nominated directors, though the alliance could not garner a majority through a democratically held election. Kolhapur Zilla Sahakari Dudh Utpadak Sangh Ltd., well known for its popular brand ‘Gokul ’, is an Operation Flood cooperative dairy project established on March 16, 1963. It is one of the most significant political and economic forces in western Maharashtra and has established itself as a prime dairy co-operative in the State. Maharashtra’s politics is shaped by the significant co-operatives’ sector.
